clinicalPearls: POLG encodes the catalytic subunit of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma; pathogenic variants impair mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) replication, producing mtDNA depletion in children and multiple mtDNA deletions in adults.

The phenotypic spectrum is a continuum spanning severe infantile Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome, childhood myocerebrohepatopathy, the MEMSA/SCAE ataxia-epilepsy phenotypes, and adult-onset progressive external ophthalmoplegia (PEO) with or without sensory ataxic neuropathy.

The clinical triad of Alpers-Huttenlocher syndrome is intractable epilepsy (often focal with epilepsia partialis continua and occipital predilection), psychomotor regression, and hepatic failure that may be precipitated or accelerated by sodium valproate.

Sodium valproate is contraindicated in POLG disease because it can trigger fulminant, frequently fatal hepatic failure; POLG testing is advised before valproate in any child with unexplained epilepsy plus liver or mitochondrial features.

Occipital-predominant seizures, cortical visual involvement, stroke-like occipital lesions and status epilepticus are characteristic of the epileptic POLG phenotypes and help distinguish them from other mitochondrial encephalopathies.

Adult POLG disease commonly presents with ptosis and PEO, sensory ataxic neuropathy, dysarthria, and may include parkinsonism, premature ovarian failure and cardiomyopathy; recessive and dominant inheritance both occur.

The most common recessive variants cluster in the linker and polymerase domains; a recurrent linker-region substitution is the single most frequent pathogenic allele and is often carried in compound heterozygosity.
Liver histology in the infantile form shows microvesicular steatosis, bile ductular proliferation, bridging fibrosis and hepatocyte dropout, distinct from primary structural liver disease.
reference.pathophysiology: POLG (chromosome 15q26) encodes POLG1, the catalytic subunit of the sole DNA polymerase responsible for replicating and repairing the mitochondrial genome, working with the POLG2 accessory subunit, the TWNK helicase and mitochondrial single-stranded binding protein. Pathogenic variants reduce polymerase processivity, proofreading (exonuclease) activity or the enzyme's interaction with template DNA, impairing faithful mtDNA synthesis. In tissues with high replicative demand and post-mitotic energy dependence this causes quantitative mtDNA depletion (prominent in infants, especially in liver, brain and muscle) or the accumulation of multiple secondary mtDNA deletions (prominent in adults). The resulting loss of mtDNA-encoded respiratory chain subunits produces a combined deficiency of complexes I, III, IV and V with relative preservation of the entirely nuclear-encoded complex II, crippling oxidative phosphorylation. Neurones, hepatocytes and skeletal muscle are especially vulnerable; in the brain the occipital and cerebellar cortices and deep grey matter show neuronal loss, spongiosis and gliosis, while the liver undergoes progressive microvesicular steatosis and fibrosis. Valproate independently inhibits mitochondrial beta-oxidation and depletes carnitine, and in the POLG-deficient liver this can tip a marginal organ into fulminant failure. Both autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant inheritance occur, the dominant forms typically producing later-onset PEO through a dominant-negative effect on the polymerase.
additionalDifferentials: Other mtDNA maintenance/depletion disorders (TWNK, DGUOK, MPV17, TK2, SUCLA2, SUCLG1, RRM2B)
MELAS and other primary mtDNA point-mutation encephalomyopathies
Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalomyopathy (MNGIE, TYMP related) in MNGIE-like presentations
Wilson disease and other metabolic causes of combined hepatic and neurological disease
Autoimmune or infective (viral) encephalitis with refractory focal seizures
Non-POLG progressive external ophthalmoplegia and myasthenic ptosis
Valproate hepatotoxicity or Reye-like syndrome from other causes
additionalInvestigations: POLG gene sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, with wider mtDNA-maintenance gene panel if negative
Blood and cerebrospinal fluid lactate, with paired plasma/CSF ratio
Muscle biopsy for respiratory chain enzymology and histochemistry (may show mosaic cytochrome-c-oxidase deficiency)
Quantitative mtDNA copy number and long-range PCR/Southern blot for mtDNA deletions in muscle or liver
Brain MRI including diffusion imaging looking for occipital and thalamic/cerebellar signal change and stroke-like lesions
EEG for occipital-predominant epileptiform activity, rhythmic high-amplitude delta with superimposed spikes, and epilepsia partialis continua
Liver function tests, coagulation profile and hepatic imaging to monitor for evolving failure
redFlags: New or worsening jaundice, coagulopathy or encephalopathy signalling impending fulminant hepatic failure, particularly after valproate exposure
Refractory status epilepticus or epilepsia partialis continua
Rapid psychomotor regression with cortical visual loss in a previously developing child
Recurrent stroke-like episodes with occipital lesions
Cardiac involvement or intractable lactic acidosis indicating multisystem decompensation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis correlates with age of onset: the infantile Alpers-Huttenlocher and myocerebrohepatopathy phenotypes are severe and usually fatal in early childhood, especially once hepatic failure or refractory epilepsy supervenes, whereas adult PEO-predominant disease is slowly progressive and compatible with prolonged survival. Care is supportive and multidisciplinary, as no disease-modifying therapy currently exists.
pitfalls: Prescribing sodium valproate for the seizures of undiagnosed POLG disease, precipitating fatal hepatic failure
Attributing early liver failure to primary hepatic disease and missing the underlying mitochondrial diagnosis
Expecting a raised lactate in every case; normal blood lactate does not exclude POLG disease, and CSF lactate may be more informative
Assuming a single autosomal recessive pattern, thereby overlooking dominantly inherited adult PEO presentations
Considering liver transplantation without recognising ongoing neurological progression, which limits its benefit

management: Avoid sodium valproate absolutely, as it can precipitate fulminant hepatic failure, and test for POLG before valproate in unexplained epilepsy with mitochondrial or hepatic features
Aggressive seizure control with valproate-sparing antiepileptic drugs, treating status epilepticus and epilepsia partialis continua in the epileptic phenotypes
Supportive multisystem management coordinated by metabolic medicine and neurology, as no curative therapy exists
Nutritional support and management of hepatic dysfunction, recognising the limited role and risks of liver transplantation in multisystem disease
Symptomatic management of ptosis and progressive external ophthalmoplegia, sensory ataxic neuropathy and dysarthria, with cardiomyopathy surveillance
Physiotherapy and mobility support, with management of parkinsonism and premature ovarian insufficiency as they arise
Genetic counselling reflecting both recessive and dominant inheritance, with family testing and reproductive advice
Escalate for acute hepatic decompensation or refractory status epilepticus
